The text is devoted to proving a relative homotopy principle for smooth maps whose singularities belong to a prescribed \({\cal K}\)-invariant class. In this setting, one considers smooth maps subject to restrictions on the types of singularities they may have, and the goal is to show that the appropriate space of such maps satisfies a relative \(h\)-principle. Roughly speaking, this means that formal or homotopical data satisfying the prescribed singularity conditions can be deformed, relative to a chosen subset, into genuine smooth maps with the required singularities.

The proof is carried out under a mild additional assumption on the chosen class of singularities. This extra condition ensures that the class behaves well enough under the constructions used in the argument, while still allowing a broad range of important examples. In particular, the \({\cal K}\)-invariance of the class guarantees that the singularity conditions are stable under the natural equivalence relation given by changes of coordinates in source and target.

After establishing the relative homotopy principle, the text turns to the study of a filtration of the group of homotopy self-equivalences of a fixed manifold \(P\). This filtration organizes the group into successive layers according to increasingly restrictive geometric or singularity-theoretic conditions. By examining these layers, one gains a more refined understanding of how homotopy self-equivalences of \(P\) can be represented or detected through maps with controlled singular behavior.

The analysis of this filtration is carried out using singularities of non-negative \({\cal K}\)-codimensions. These singularities provide a natural hierarchy: lower-codimension singularities appear more generically, while higher-codimension singularities impose stronger restrictions. By relating the stages of the filtration to such singularity classes, the text connects the topology of the homotopy self-equivalence group with the geometry of smooth maps and their allowable singularities.

The text studies a relative version of the homotopy principle for smooth maps whose singularities are restricted to lie in a prescribed class. More precisely, it considers smooth maps into a manifold \(P\) whose local singularity types belong to a given \({\cal K}\)-invariant set, where \({\cal K}\)-equivalence is the standard equivalence relation on map-germs induced by changes of coordinates in the source and target. The main question is whether formal solutions satisfying these singularity restrictions can be deformed, relative to a prescribed subset, into genuine smooth maps with the same allowed singularities.

Under a mild additional hypothesis on the chosen \({\cal K}\)-invariant class, the text proves that such a relative homotopy principle holds. The argument is formulated in terms of singularity classes and their \({\cal K}\)-codimensions, which measure the complexity of a singularity inside the appropriate jet space. By organizing singularities according to these codimensions, the proof gives a systematic way to pass from formal data to actual maps while preserving the prescribed singularity constraints and the relative conditions.

After establishing the relative homotopy principle, the text applies it to the study of the homotopy self-equivalence group of a manifold \(P\). In particular, singularities of non-negative \({\cal K}\)-codimension are used to construct a natural filtration of this group. This filtration reflects how self-equivalences of \(P\) can be detected or organized by the types of singularities allowed in associated smooth maps. Thus, the results connect the local classification of singularities with global questions about the structure of manifold self-equivalences.

Overall, the work shows that singularity theory, and especially the language of \({\cal K}\)-invariant classes and \({\cal K}\)-codimension, provides a powerful framework for proving homotopy principles and for extracting algebraic and topological information about manifolds.
